unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 7: Success, Careers, and Personal Growth. In this unit you will explore what it means to succeed, how people build meaningful careers, and how personal growth shapes the choices we make. You will read about real-world career paths, discuss what makes a person truly successful, and discover that success is not only about money or fame — it is also about dedication, resilience, and the contribution you make to your community.
unit.learningPath: Begin with the Vocabulary section and learn the twenty-three unit words a few at a time, saying each example sentence aloud. Work through the six grammar lessons on adjective + preposition combinations, verb patterns with infinitives and gerunds, and the passive voice. Read “Building a Future”, the careers interview with Nurse Sana, and the three-part story “The Storm of Truth”, answering the comprehension questions with evidence from the text. Complete the writing workshop, the speaking tasks and the activities, then finish with the quiz and the Check Your Learning self-assessment.

readings.title: Building a Future
readings.setting: Careers and communities across East Africa
readings.passageScript:
In communities across East Africa, young people are discovering that success does not always follow a single path. Some become doctors or engineers after years of study. Others find their vocation through hands-on work, learning a trade as an apprentice beside an experienced craftsperson. What matters most is not the title you hold but the dedication you bring to your work and the contribution you make to the people around you.
Imani, a seventeen-year-old from a small town near Garowe, always dreamed of becoming a teacher. Her family did not have much money, but Imani was determined to succeed. She studied by lamplight every evening, and her perseverance impressed everyone who knew her. When she passed her exams with distinction, the entire neighbourhood celebrated. “I am proud of what I have achieved,” Imani told a local reporter, “but I am even more grateful for the people who helped me along the way.”
Imani’s story shows that ambition alone is not enough. She was supported by her mother, who sold vegetables at the market to pay for books. She was encouraged by a teacher who stayed after school to give extra lessons. And she was inspired by a visiting speaker who said, “Every great career begins with a single step of courage.” That speaker was herself once a young girl from a rural village who went on to become a university professor.
Not far from Imani’s town, a young man named Tariq chose a different route. He was always fascinated by machines and electronics. Instead of attending university, he became an apprentice at a small repair shop. His mentor taught him to fix radios, solar panels, and mobile phones. Within two years, Tariq had saved enough money to open his own workshop. Today he is a successful entrepreneur who employs three other young people.
“People told me that working with my hands was not a real profession,” Tariq said. “But I am passionate about what I do, and my business helps the community. Solar panels are repaired here. Phones are fixed here. Jobs are created here.” He paused and added, “Success is not measured by a certificate on the wall. It is measured by the lives you improve.”
Both Imani and Tariq show that success requires resilience. Imani faced nights without electricity and months without new textbooks. Tariq was criticised by people who thought his work was unimportant. But both kept going because they were committed to their goals and responsible for their own futures.
A career counsellor at a secondary school in Hargeisa explains: “We teach our students that there are many kinds of success. A doctor saves lives. A farmer feeds families. A builder creates homes. An artist inspires hearts. Each profession deserves respect, and each person’s aspiration is valid. What we encourage is that students find something they are interested in, work hard at it, and never stop learning.”
The counsellor also stresses the importance of mentorship. “Young people need guides,” she says. “A good mentor does not tell you what to do — they help you discover what you are capable of. When someone believes in you, you start to believe in yourself.”
Today, new opportunities are opening up across the region. Young women are being trained in technology. Boys and girls are being prepared for careers that did not exist ten years ago. Community centres offer workshops where teenagers can explore different trades, practise public speaking, and develop their own business ideas.
Whether you dream of teaching, engineering, farming, medicine, business, or the arts, the message is the same: success is built step by step, through dedication, perseverance, and a willingness to learn from every milestone along the way.

readings.title: An Interview About Careers
readings.passageScript:
A local radio reporter visited the district hospital to interview Nurse Sana about her career.
Interviewer: Tell us about your work.
Sana: I am a nurse at the district hospital. I have been working here for six years. I was trained in Mogadishu, and then I was sent to this hospital to help the community.
Interviewer: What made you choose nursing?
Sana: I was always interested in helping people. When I was twelve, my grandmother became ill, and I watched the nurses care for her. I was amazed by their skill and kindness. That day, I decided to become a nurse.
Interviewer: What has been the hardest part?
Sana: The training was very difficult. I had to study for four years, and I often felt like giving up. But I kept going because I was committed to my dream. My family was supportive of me, and my teacher always said, “Do not stop. You are capable of great things.”
Interviewer: What advice would you give to young people?
Sana: Find something you are passionate about. Do not be afraid of hard work. And always be grateful for the people who help you along the way. Success is not a destination — it is a journey.

readings.title: The Storm of Truth, part 1
readings.setting: A coastal secondary school as a storm approaches
readings.passageScript:
The sky above Lamu was heavy with grey clouds when Amal arrived at school that Monday morning. The wind carried the sharp smell of salt from the Indian Ocean, and the palm trees along the road swayed as if they were whispering a warning.
“Something big is coming,” said her classmate, Sami, looking up at the darkening sky. “The fishermen pulled their boats in early.”
But Amal was not thinking about the weather. Her mind was fixed on something else entirely: the Regional Young Leaders Competition. The winner would receive a scholarship to attend a special leadership academy in Nairobi — a milestone that could change her life forever.
“I have been preparing for this for months,” Amal told Sami. “My speech is about how young people can build careers that serve their communities.”
“You are dedicated to this,” Sami said, nodding. “I have never seen anyone work so hard.”
Amal smiled, but inside she felt the weight of expectation. Her family was proud of her ambition, and her mother had told her, “We are grateful for every opportunity you earn. Make the most of it.”
At school, their English teacher, Teacher Yasmin, announced some news.
“The competition semi-final is this Friday,” she said. “Three students from our school have been selected: Amal, Sami, and Nora. You will each give a five-minute speech in front of a panel of judges.”
Amal glanced at Nora. They had been friends since childhood, but recently something had changed. Nora had become distant and secretive. She carried a folder everywhere and would not show anyone what was inside.
“I am committed to winning,” Nora said quietly. “This qualification could open doors for me.”
That evening, Amal worked on her speech at the community centre. The centre had been established by a retired teacher called Mr. Nadir, who now served as a mentor to the town’s young people. His small office was filled with books, maps, and photographs of students who had gone on to become doctors, engineers, and teachers.
“Mentorship is about more than advice,” Mr. Nadir had once told them. “It is about helping someone discover what they are capable of.”
Amal read her speech aloud to him. It was about how entrepreneurship could lift communities out of poverty, and how young apprentices could learn skills that schools did not always teach.
“Good structure,” Mr. Nadir said. “But I want you to add something personal. Talk about your own aspiration. What drives you? Why does this matter to you, Amal?”
She nodded and wrote a new paragraph that night. In it she described watching her mother sell fruit at the harbour, working from dawn until dusk, and how that resilience had taught her that success was not given — it was built.
On Tuesday, the storm warnings grew louder. The administration announced that all after-school activities would be cancelled if the weather worsened. Rain began to fall in bursts, and the harbour was closed.
But inside the school, a different kind of storm was brewing.
During lunch, Amal went to the library to return a book. As she turned the corner between the shelves, she heard voices. Nora was speaking to someone on the phone.
“Yes, I have it,” Nora said. “The speech is very good. I just changed a few words so it does not look exactly the same. No one will know.”

readings.title: The Storm of Truth, part 2
readings.setting: A coastal town during the storm
readings.passageScript:
Amal froze. Her heart hammered in her chest.
Nora looked up and saw her. For a moment, neither of them spoke.
“Amal — it is not what you think,” Nora started.
“Whose speech did you copy?” Amal asked, her voice steady but low.
Nora’s eyes dropped. “It was found online. A speech by a student in Tanzania who won a competition two years ago. I changed some sentences. I — I did not have time to write my own.”
“You could have asked for help,” Amal said. “Teacher Yasmin would have helped you. Mr. Nadir would have helped you.”
“I was afraid of looking weak,” Nora whispered. “Everyone expects me to be brilliant. My family keeps telling me I must win. I was worried about disappointing them.”
Amal felt a mix of anger and sadness. She understood the pressure. She felt it too. But she also knew that integrity mattered more than any prize.
“If you give that speech,” Amal said gently, “and someone discovers the truth later, everything you have worked for will be lost. Your reputation will be damaged. Is that worth it?”
Nora was silent for a long time. Then she said, “What should I do?”
“Write your own speech,” Amal said. “You still have three days. I will help you.”
That evening, the storm arrived in full force. Thunder cracked across the sky, and rain battered the rooftops of Lamu. The power went out across the entire town. Families gathered in their homes with candles and oil lamps, waiting for the weather to pass.
But in Amal’s house, something remarkable was happening. By the glow of a kerosene lamp, Amal and Nora sat together at the kitchen table, writing.
“Tell me what you are passionate about,” Amal said.
“The sea,” Nora replied. “I love the ocean. I want to study marine science. I want to protect the coral reefs and the fish that our community depends on.”
“Then that is your speech,” Amal said.
Over the next two days, Nora wrote and rewrote her speech. She practised it in front of Mr. Nadir, who gave her honest feedback. She was encouraged by his words: “This is real. This is you. A speech is valued for its truth, not its polish.”
On Thursday evening, the storm finally passed. The sky cleared, and the stars appeared over the ocean. The town began to clean up: fallen branches were removed by neighbours, damaged market stalls were repaired by shopkeepers, and the school hall was prepared for the competition the next day.
Friday morning arrived bright and warm. The judges — a university professor, a local business leader, and a journalist — sat at a long table in the school hall. Students from five schools had gathered.
Sami spoke first. His speech was about the importance of vocational training and how apprenticeships could help young people who could not afford university. He was confident in his message and spoke with clear distinction.
Then Nora took the stage. Her hands were shaking, but her voice was strong.
“My name is Nora, and I am fascinated by the ocean,” she began. “Every day, I watch the fishermen go out, and I wonder: what is happening beneath the surface? Our reefs are dying. Our fish are disappearing. And not enough young people are being trained in marine science to help.”

readings.title: The Storm of Truth, part 3
readings.setting: The school hall after the storm
readings.passageScript:
She spoke about her dream to study coral ecosystems, about the contribution she wanted to make, and about the moment she almost lost her way.
“I nearly gave a speech that was not mine,” she said quietly. The hall went still. “But a true friend reminded me that integrity is the foundation of every real achievement. I am standing here today because I chose to be honest. And that, to me, is already a kind of success.”
The applause was loud and long.
Finally, Amal stepped up. She spoke about her mother, about entrepreneurship, about how every profession deserves respect. She spoke about perseverance — how she had written her speech seven times before she was satisfied with it.
“Success is not a single moment,” she said. “It is not a trophy or a certificate. It is the dedication you show every day. It is the gratitude you feel for those who help you. And it is the initiative you take when no one is watching.”
When the judges announced the results, Amal was named the winner. But as she stepped forward to accept the certificate, she looked back at Nora and smiled.
Later, Mr. Nadir found them both under the old mango tree in the playground.
“You were both brave today,” he said. “Nora, you were brave because you told the truth. Amal, you were brave because you helped your friend instead of protecting your advantage.”
“Is that not what mentorship is?” Amal asked.
Mr. Nadir laughed. “I think the student is now teaching the teacher.”
That night, the ocean was calm. The storm had passed, and the truth had held.
Amal wrote one last line in her notebook before sleep:
“The storm tested us. But the truth held us steady. Every achievement built on integrity is a milestone that no wind can blow away.”

comprehension.question: According to the opening of “Building a Future”, what matters most about the work a person does?
comprehension.correctAnswer: What matters most is not the title you hold but the dedication you bring to your work and the contribution you make to the people around you.
comprehension.explanation: The opening paragraph says it directly: 'What matters most is not the title you hold but the dedication you bring to your work and the contribution you make to the people around you.'

comprehension.question: What did Imani dream of becoming, and what evidence shows that the journey was difficult for her?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Imani dreamed of becoming a teacher; her family did not have much money, she studied by lamplight every evening, and she faced nights without electricity and months without new textbooks.
comprehension.explanation: The text says Imani always dreamed of becoming a teacher. Her family did not have much money, she studied by lamplight every evening, and later the writer adds that she faced nights without electricity and months without new textbooks.

comprehension.question: Where was Sana trained, and what work does she do now?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Sana was trained in Mogadishu and now works as a nurse at the district hospital, where she has been for six years.
comprehension.explanation: In her first answer, Sana says, 'I am a nurse at the district hospital. I have been working here for six years. I was trained in Mogadishu,' so both facts come straight from her own words.

comprehension.question: What prize would the winner of the Regional Young Leaders Competition receive?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The winner would receive a scholarship to attend a special leadership academy in Nairobi.
comprehension.explanation: When the story introduces the Regional Young Leaders Competition, it says the winner would receive a scholarship to attend a special leadership academy in Nairobi, a milestone that could change Amal's life.

comprehension.question: How did Tariq answer the people who said that working with his hands was not a real profession?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Tariq said he is passionate about what he does and that his business helps the community, because solar panels are repaired, phones are fixed and jobs are created in his workshop; he added that success is measured by the lives you improve, not by a certificate on the wall.
comprehension.explanation: You must select Tariq's own quoted words as evidence and explain the viewpoint they express about the value of practical work.

comprehension.question: What three pieces of advice does Sana give to young people at the end of the interview?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She tells them to find something they are passionate about, not to be afraid of hard work, and always to be grateful for the people who help them along the way.

comprehension.correctAnswer: Nora had become distant and secretive, she carried a folder everywhere and would not show anyone what was inside, and she said quietly that she was committed to winning.
comprehension.explanation: When Amal glances at Nora, the text says Nora had become distant and secretive, carried a folder everywhere and would not show anyone what was inside, and said quietly that she was committed to winning.

comprehension.correctAnswer: She said the speech was found online, that she did not have time to write her own, that she was afraid of looking weak, and that she was worried about disappointing her family, who kept telling her she must win.

comprehension.question: According to Amal, what could Nora lose if she gave the copied speech and the truth was discovered later?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Amal warned that everything Nora had worked for would be lost and that her reputation would be damaged, which is why she asked whether the prize was worth that risk.
comprehension.explanation: Amal tells Nora that if someone discovers the truth later, 'everything you have worked for will be lost. Your reputation will be damaged,' and then asks, 'Is that worth it?'

comprehension.correctAnswer: Nora admitted that she nearly gave a speech that was not hers; she called her honesty a kind of success because a true friend reminded her that integrity is the foundation of every real achievement, and standing there honestly proved she had chosen the harder, better path.

comprehension.question: Under the mango tree, how did Mr. Nadir say each girl had been brave?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He said Nora was brave because she told the truth, and Amal was brave because she helped her friend instead of protecting her advantage.
comprehension.explanation: Under the mango tree Mr. Nadir says, 'Nora, you were brave because you told the truth. Amal, you were brave because you helped your friend instead of protecting your advantage.'

comprehension.question: Explain the meaning of Amal’s final notebook line: “Every achievement built on integrity is a milestone that no wind can blow away.”
comprehension.correctAnswer: She means that success earned honestly is permanent: pressure, gossip or setbacks, like the storm, cannot destroy an achievement that rests on truth, while a prize won by cheating can be lost the moment the truth appears.
comprehension.explanation: The storm in the story could not shake the girls' honesty, and Nora's copied speech would have been lost if the truth came out. So Amal means honest success lasts, while a prize won by cheating can be blown away.

grammar.title: Adjective + Preposition — The Basics
grammar.explanation: Many English adjectives must be followed by one fixed partner preposition: we say interested in, never interested about, and proud of, never proud for. Learning each pair as a single phrase makes your writing about success and careers sound natural and accurate.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Adjective + OF: proud of — She is proud of her results. capable of — You are capable of achieving great things. aware of — He is aware of the difficulties ahead. afraid of — Do not be afraid of making mistakes. fond of — I am fond of reading about famous scientists. ashamed of — There is nothing to be ashamed of in asking for help.
Adjective + IN: interested in — She is interested in studying law. involved in — He is involved in the school’s career fair. skilled in — She is skilled in public speaking. successful in — He was successful in starting his business. confident in — I am confident in my abilities.
Adjective + FOR: responsible for — You are responsible for your own progress. famous for — The city is famous for its universities. grateful for — I am grateful for my teacher’s guidance. prepared for — Are you prepared for the exam? qualified for — She is qualified for the position.
Adjective + TO: dedicated to — He is dedicated to his studies. committed to — She is committed to helping others. related to — This lesson is related to career planning. accustomed to — She is accustomed to working long hours. used to — She is used to hard work.
Adjective + BY, ABOUT or WITH: amazed by — We were amazed by her achievement. inspired by — He was inspired by his grandfather’s story. fascinated by — She is fascinated by marine science. worried about — He is worried about the future. passionate about — She is passionate about teaching. satisfied with — I am satisfied with my progress. disappointed with — He was disappointed with his results.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often write “I am interested about science” or “She is proud for her daughter”, borrowing a preposition that feels logical. The pairs are fixed: it must be interested in science and proud of her daughter.
grammar.memoryTip: Learn each pair as one mini phrase on a flashcard: adjective on the front, preposition plus an example sentence on the back, and test yourself daily.
grammar.practice:
Part A — Complete each sentence with the correct preposition (of, in, for, to, by, about or with): 1) She is very proud ______ her brother’s success. 2) We are interested ______ learning about different careers. 3) He is responsible ______ organising the school event. 4) I am grateful ______ the support I received. 5) They were amazed ______ the speaker’s story. 6) She is dedicated ______ becoming a doctor. 7) He was disappointed ______ his performance in the exam. 8) Are you prepared ______ the interview tomorrow?
Part B — Complete these sentences the same way: 1) The teacher is dedicated ______ helping every student succeed. 2) We were amazed ______ the speaker’s life story. 3) She was disappointed ______ her exam results, but she did not give up. 4) He is passionate ______ working with technology. 5) I am grateful ______ the mentorship I received from my teacher. 6) She is proud ______ her community’s achievements. 7) Are you prepared ______ the challenges of starting a business?
Part C — One more round: 1) She is very proud ______ her sister’s achievement. 2) I am interested ______ studying medicine. 3) He is responsible ______ looking after the younger students. 4) We are grateful ______ the help we received. 5) The students were inspired ______ the guest speaker. 6) She is dedicated ______ becoming a great teacher.

Self-Check Answer Key (read after you finish the exercise, not before): Part A — 1) of 2) in 3) for 4) for 5) by 6) to 7) with 8) for. Part B — 1) to 2) by 3) with 4) about 5) for 6) of 7) for. Part C — 1) of 2) in 3) for 4) for 5) by 6) to. Every answer follows the fixed adjective + preposition pairs listed in Rule and Examples above (proud OF, interested IN, responsible FOR, grateful FOR, amazed BY, dedicated TO, disappointed WITH, prepared FOR, passionate ABOUT, inspired BY).

grammar.title: Adjective + Preposition — Advanced Uses
grammar.explanation: A preposition is always followed by a noun or a gerund, never by an infinitive, so any verb that comes after an adjective + preposition pair must take the -ing form. In questions, the preposition stays glued to its adjective at the end.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Adjective + preposition + gerund: She is good at solving problems (never “good at to solve”). He is interested in becoming an engineer. I am tired of waiting for results. She is responsible for looking after the library. He is committed to improving his grades. We are excited about starting the new project.
Adjective + preposition in questions — the preposition stays with the adjective: What are you interested in? Who is responsible for this project? What are you afraid of? What is she passionate about?
grammar.commonMistake: Writing “I am interested in to study medicine” puts an infinitive after a preposition. Because prepositions only accept nouns or gerunds, the correct form is “I am interested in studying medicine”.
grammar.memoryTip: Preposition + verb? Add -ing. Say the rule aloud every time you meet one of these pairs until choosing the gerund becomes automatic.
grammar.practice:
Part A — Complete each sentence using the -ing form of the verb in brackets: 1) She is good at ______ (solve) difficult maths problems. 2) He is interested in ______ (become) a pilot. 3) I am tired of ______ (hear) excuses. 4) They are excited about ______ (visit) the new science lab. 5) She is responsible for ______ (manage) the team. 6) Are you used to ______ (wake) up early for school? 7) He is committed to ______ (learn) a new skill every month. 8) What are you passionate about ______ (do) in the future?

Self-Check Answer Key: Part A — 1) solving 2) becoming 3) hearing 4) visiting 5) managing 6) waking 7) learning 8) doing. Every verb takes the -ing form because it follows a preposition (at, in, of, about, to), and a preposition can only be followed by a noun or a gerund, never an infinitive.

grammar.title: Verb Patterns — Infinitive and Gerund
grammar.explanation: When one verb follows another, the second verb takes a fixed form: some verbs demand the infinitive with to, others demand the gerund, and a small group accepts both with a change of meaning. Choosing the right pattern is essential when you write about plans, ambitions and experiences.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Verbs followed by the infinitive: want — I want to become a teacher. hope — She hopes to win the scholarship. decide — He decided to study harder. plan — We plan to visit the university. agree — They agreed to work together. learn — She learned to code last year. promise — He promised to help his classmates. offer — The teacher offered to stay after school. refuse — She refused to give up. manage — He managed to pass the exam.
Verbs followed by the gerund: enjoy — She enjoys reading biographies. practise — He practises speaking every day. avoid — Try to avoid wasting time. consider — Have you considered changing careers? finish — I finished writing my application. keep — Keep trying until you succeed. suggest — She suggested starting a study group. mind — Would you mind helping me? miss — I miss living near the school. deny — He denied copying the homework.
Verbs that take both, with different meanings: remember to do means do not forget (“Remember to bring your CV to the interview.”), while remember doing recalls a past event (“I remember meeting the principal for the first time.”). Stop to do means pause in order to do something else (“He stopped to help a younger student.”), while stop doing means quit (“She stopped worrying and took action.”). Try to do means attempt something difficult (“I tried to solve the puzzle.”), while try doing means experiment (“Try using a dictionary for new words.”).
grammar.commonMistake: Learners write “I enjoy to read books” or “She decided studying medicine”, swapping the two patterns. Enjoy always takes the gerund and decide always takes the infinitive: I enjoy reading; she decided to study.
grammar.memoryTip: Keep two growing lists in the back of your notebook, one headed TO and one headed -ING, and add every new verb to the correct list the day you meet it.
grammar.practice:
Part A — Choose the correct form: 1) She wants ______ (to become / becoming) a scientist. 2) He enjoys ______ (to teach / teaching) children. 3) They decided ______ (to move / moving) to the city. 4) I finished ______ (to write / writing) my essay. 5) He offered ______ (to carry / carrying) the heavy books. 6) She suggested ______ (to start / starting) a book club. 7) I remember ______ (to visit / visiting) my grandmother when I was young. 8) Please remember ______ (to lock / locking) the door when you leave.
Part B — Choose again: 1) She hopes ______ (to study / studying) engineering at university. 2) He enjoys ______ (to teach / teaching) younger children. 3) They decided ______ (to move / moving) to the city for better opportunities. 4) I keep ______ (to practise / practising) until I get it right. 5) She promised ______ (to finish / finishing) the project by Friday. 6) Have you considered ______ (to become / becoming) a doctor? 7) He stopped ______ (to rest / resting) for a few minutes before continuing. 8) I remember ______ (to meet / meeting) her at the career fair last year.
Part C — Final round: 1) She wants ______ (to become / becoming) a nurse. 2) He enjoys ______ (to help / helping) others. 3) They decided ______ (to open / opening) a new business. 4) I practise ______ (to speak / speaking) English every morning. 5) Remember ______ (to bring / bringing) your notes to the meeting. 6) She keeps ______ (to try / trying) even when things are hard.

Self-Check Answer Key: Part A — 1) to become 2) teaching 3) to move 4) writing 5) to carry 6) starting 7) visiting 8) to lock. Part B — 1) to study 2) teaching 3) to move 4) practising 5) to finish 6) becoming 7) to rest 8) meeting. Part C — 1) to become 2) helping 3) to open 4) speaking 5) to bring 6) trying. Reasoning: want, decide, hope, offer and promise all take the infinitive; enjoy, finish, suggest, keep and practise all take the gerund. In Part A item 7 and Part B item 8, remember + gerund is used because the sentence recalls a past event (I remember visiting/meeting...); in Part A item 8 and Part C item 5, remember/an imperative + infinitive is used because it means not to forget a future action (remember to lock/bring...). In Part B item 7, stopped to rest means paused in order to rest, not quit resting, which fits “for a few minutes before continuing.”

grammar.title: Passive Voice
grammar.explanation: The passive voice puts the spotlight on the action or its receiver instead of the doer, which is why it fills formal writing, news reports and descriptions of achievements. It is formed with be in the correct tense plus the past participle, and the doer can be added with by or simply left out.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Present simple passive: “The award is given to the top student every year.” “Applications are reviewed by the committee.”
Past simple passive: “The school was built in 1995.” “She was awarded a scholarship.”
Present continuous passive: “New classrooms are being built this month.” “Students are being trained in new skills.”
Present perfect passive: “The winner has been announced.” “The road has been repaired.”
Use the passive when the action matters more than the doer (“The roads were repaired last month.”), when the doer is unknown (“My phone was stolen yesterday.”), when describing processes (“Applications are reviewed by the committee.”) and in formal writing (“Students are expected to arrive on time.”).
To change active to passive: make the object the new subject, change the verb to be + past participle in the same tense, then move the old subject into a by phrase or drop it. Active: “The committee chose the winner.” Passive: “The winner was chosen by the committee.”
grammar.commonMistake: Two slips spoil most passives: the wrong participle, as in “The prize was give to Nora” instead of “was given”, and the wrong form of be, as in “The students is taught by Teacher Yasmin” instead of “are taught”.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of the passive as moving the spotlight: in “The cake was eaten” the cake is lit up; in “She ate the cake” the eater is. Choose whichever the sentence should shine on.
grammar.practice:
Part A — Rewrite each sentence in the passive voice: 1) The judges selected three finalists. 2) The school offers free career workshops. 3) A local businessman has sponsored the competition. 4) They are building a new science laboratory. 5) The headteacher will announce the results tomorrow. 6) The community centre trained fifty young people last year.
Part B — Rewrite these as well: 1) The school gave Amal a scholarship. 2) The community supports young entrepreneurs. 3) A famous speaker inspired the students. 4) They are building new classrooms. 5) Someone has offered her a job.
Part C — And these: 1) The company trained five new apprentices last month. 2) The committee has chosen the winner. 3) People admire her dedication. 4) They are offering free workshops to teenagers. 5) A local businessman sponsors the youth programme.
Part D — Detective work: find three passive voice sentences in “Building a Future” or “The Storm of Truth”, name the tense of each one, and rewrite each in the active voice.

Self-Check Answer Key: Part A — 1) Three finalists were selected (by the judges). [past simple passive] 2) Free career workshops are offered (by the school). [present simple passive] 3) The competition has been sponsored by a local businessman. [present perfect passive] 4) A new science laboratory is being built. [present continuous passive] 5) The results will be announced (by the headteacher) tomorrow. [future passive: will + be + past participle] 6) Fifty young people were trained by the community centre last year. [past simple passive]
Part B — 1) Amal was given a scholarship (by the school). [past simple passive] 2) Young entrepreneurs are supported by the community. [present simple passive] 3) The students were inspired by a famous speaker. [past simple passive] 4) New classrooms are being built. [present continuous passive] 5) She has been offered a job. [present perfect passive]
Part C — 1) Five new apprentices were trained by the company last month. [past simple passive] 2) The winner has been chosen by the committee. [present perfect passive] 3) Her dedication is admired (by people). [present simple passive — the vague agent “by people” is usually dropped: “Her dedication is admired.”] 4) Free workshops are being offered to teenagers. [present continuous passive] 5) The youth programme is sponsored by a local businessman. [present simple passive]
Part D — this asks you to find sentences in this unit's own reading passages, so check your finds against these three confirmed examples rather than an invented list: 1) “She was supported by her mother, who sold vegetables at the market to pay for books” (Building a Future) — past simple passive; active: “Her mother, who sold vegetables at the market to pay for books, supported her.” 2) “The centre had been established by a retired teacher called Mr. Nadir” (The Storm of Truth, part 1) — past perfect passive; active: “A retired teacher called Mr. Nadir had established the centre.” 3) “Fallen branches were removed by neighbours” (The Storm of Truth, part 2) — past simple passive; active: “Neighbours removed fallen branches.” Other correct finds include “Three students from our school have been selected” (present perfect passive) and “Young women are being trained in technology” (present continuous passive), both from the same two stories.

grammar.title: Putting It All Together
grammar.explanation: Real writing combines several grammar features in one text, so this lesson practises weaving adjective + preposition pairs, verb patterns and the passive voice together, exactly as the Writing Workshop biography will demand.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Read this paragraph and notice how the three features work together:
“Alina is a young woman who is passionate about helping her community. She decided to train as a teacher because she enjoys working with children. After three years of hard work, she was awarded a teaching certificate. She is now responsible for a class of forty students. She is proud of what she has achieved, and she is committed to improving education in her town. New textbooks have been provided by a charity, and a computer room is being built this month.”
In the paragraph, find four adjective + preposition combinations, two verb patterns (one infinitive, one gerund) and two passive voice sentences before you write your own.
grammar.commonMistake: When combining features, learners often mix the rules, producing “She is interested to become a doctor”. The preposition still demands a gerund even in a long sentence: “She is interested in becoming a doctor”.
grammar.memoryTip: Draft first, then colour-code: underline adjective + preposition pairs, circle verb patterns and highlight passives, and any sentence with no marks probably needs another look.
grammar.practice:
Write your own paragraph of six to eight sentences about a person, real or imagined, who has achieved something great. Include at least three different adjective + preposition combinations, at least two verb patterns (one with the infinitive and one with the gerund), at least two passive voice sentences, and at least three vocabulary words from this unit.

Self-Check (this task is open-ended writing, so there is no single correct paragraph — use this model and checklist to judge your own work instead): Model paragraph — “Farah is a young woman who is passionate about marine conservation. She decided to study environmental science because she wanted to protect the coral reefs near her home. Her ambition pushed her to keep going even when funding was difficult to find. She enjoys teaching younger students about the ocean, and she is proud of the changes her project has brought to her town. Two years ago, a small research grant was given to her by a local charity, and a new coastal classroom has now been built with her guidance. Her dedication and perseverance are responsible for the whole community's new respect for the sea.” Checklist — count in your own paragraph: at least 3 different adjective + preposition pairs (the model uses passionate about, proud of, responsible for); at least one infinitive verb pattern (decided to study) and one gerund verb pattern (enjoys teaching); at least 2 passive voice sentences in a correct, matching tense (was given...by, has now been built); at least 3 vocabulary words from this unit (the model uses ambition, dedication, perseverance); and 6 to 8 sentences total about a real or imagined person who achieved something great.

grammar.title: Grade 7 Editing and Application
grammar.explanation: Strong Grade 7 writers treat the first draft as raw material: they reread whole paragraphs to check that every adjective + preposition pair, verb pattern and passive form still carries the intended meaning, then revise one feature at a time.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Editing routine for this unit: read your biography or career presentation aloud one sentence at a time. Check that every adjective has its correct partner preposition, that every second verb is in the right infinitive or -ing form, and that every passive uses be plus the past participle in the matching tense. Example edit: “She was interested about medicine and decided studying hard” becomes “She was interested in medicine and decided to study hard.”
grammar.commonMistake: Fixing the grammar but flattening the meaning: “The award was won” says far less than “The regional award was won by a first-year apprentice”. Keep the informative detail while you correct the form.
grammar.memoryTip: Read, notice, revise, reread — and give each editing pass exactly one grammar feature to hunt for.
grammar.practice:
Take your draft from the Writing Workshop and complete three editing passes: pass one checks every adjective + preposition pair, pass two checks every verb pattern, and pass three checks every passive sentence. Mark eight changes in the margin, then explain in two sentences how your revisions improved the clarity of the piece.

Self-Check Method (this task edits your own Writing Workshop draft, so there is no fixed answer key to match — use this three-pass routine and worked examples to judge your edits instead): Pass 1, adjective + preposition — check every adjective keeps its one fixed partner preposition from this unit's Grammar Lessons 1 and 2. Worked example: “She was interested about medicine” becomes “She was interested in medicine.” Pass 2, verb pattern — check every second verb is in the correct infinitive or -ing form for the verb before it. Worked example: “decided studying hard” becomes “decided to study hard.” Pass 3, passive voice — check every passive sentence uses be in the matching tense plus the past participle, and that fixing the grammar has not deleted useful detail. Worked example: “The prize was give to Nora” becomes “The prize was given to Nora”, not the thinner “The prize was given.” Your 8 margin changes should sort cleanly into these three passes, and your two-sentence explanation should describe how each fix changed meaning or clarity, not just that you “corrected the grammar.”

Whichever option you choose, include at least two adjective + preposition combinations, at least two passive voice sentences, one verb pattern and five unit vocabulary words, then check every sentence against the editing checklist before you finish.
writing.modelText: The person I admire most is my uncle, Rohan. He grew up in a small village and was determined to build a better life for his family. Although he was faced with many difficulties, including poverty and the loss of his father at a young age, he never gave up. He was inspired by his mother, who taught him the value of perseverance and hard work. Today, Rohan is a respected entrepreneur who runs a successful transport business and employs more than twenty people.
writing.sentenceStarter: The person I admire most is...

items: Introduction: The person I admire most is my aunt, Faiza, a woman known throughout our neighbourhood for her integrity and her refusal to cut corners, even when nobody was watching.

Early life and challenges, verb pattern: She grew up in a crowded refugee camp and was often anxious about whether her family would have enough to eat that week. Despite these hardships, she decided to open a small tailoring business instead of waiting for someone else to offer her a job, relying on sheer perseverance to learn the trade from a retired seamstress.

Achievements, passive voice: She was awarded a small business grant at the age of twenty-two, and her shop was later featured in a regional newspaper as proof of what resilience can achieve when talent meets hard work — a milestone she still keeps framed on her wall.
Legacy and closing: Today, Faiza mentors five young apprentices herself, and her legacy proves that anyone capable of persevering through hardship can eventually build a life worth admiring.
otherAnswers: A learner choosing Option B (Career Presentation) might instead open with "My dream job is to become a paediatric nurse," describe the qualifications required, explain in the passive voice how sick children are cared for, and close with steps such as "I plan to study biology and volunteer at a clinic first."

Another Option B learner might choose marine engineering, describing how coastal communities are protected by well-built harbours, and listing verb-pattern steps such as "I intend to study physics and hope to complete an internship on a research vessel."

writing.successCriteria: I chose one option and followed its four-paragraph structure; used two adjective + preposition combinations; included two passive voice sentences and one verb pattern; used five unit vocabulary words; checked capital letters and punctuation with the editing checklist
writing.support: Plan one paragraph at a time using the structure headings, and borrow sentence shapes from the model paragraph before writing your own.
writing.extension: Add a short quotation from your subject or an imagined interview line, and vary your sentence openers so no two paragraphs begin the same way.

writing.title: Writing 2: A Thank-You Letter from Nora
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Imagine you are Nora on the evening after the competition. Write a thank-you letter to Amal of six to eight sentences explaining what the experience taught you about integrity and friendship. Use at least two adjective + preposition combinations and at least two vocabulary words from this unit, and close with one sentence about your plans to study the ocean.
writing.modelText: Dear Amal, I am grateful for the courage you showed me this week. I was so worried about disappointing my family that I almost lost something more valuable than any prize. You reminded me that integrity is the foundation of every real achievement. Thanks to you, I stood before the judges with a speech that was truly mine. I am now committed to studying marine science and protecting our reefs. Your friend always, Nora.
writing.sentenceStarter: Dear Amal, I am grateful for...
writing.expectedLength: One organised letter of two short paragraphs

items: Dear Amal, I am grateful for the courage you showed me this week. I was so worried about disappointing my family that I almost lost something more valuable than any prize. You reminded me that integrity is the foundation of every real achievement, and I am ashamed of how close I came to forgetting that.

Thanks to you, I stood before the judges with a speech that was truly mine, and the audience believed every word because it was honest. I am now committed to studying marine science and protecting our reefs, the way we always said we would. Your friend always, Nora.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote in Nora's voice; explained what the experience taught her; used two adjective + preposition combinations; included two unit vocabulary words; ended with her plan for the future
writing.support: Reread the confrontation scene and Nora's speech first, then list three things she learned before turning them into letter sentences.
writing.extension: Add one sentence in the passive voice about how the speech was rewritten, and a postscript that looks forward to next year's competition.

writing.title: Writing 3: My Motto for Success
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Amal wrote, “Every achievement built on integrity is a milestone that no wind can blow away.” Write your own motto about success or personal growth in one memorable sentence, then write one paragraph of five to seven sentences explaining what your motto means, where it came from, and how it could guide your choices at school this year. Use at least three unit vocabulary words.
writing.modelText: My motto is: “Small steps taken daily carry you further than giant leaps taken once.” I chose it because perseverance matters more to me than sudden luck. When my reading was weak, daily practice slowly rebuilt my confidence. The motto reminds me that every milestone is reached one step at a time. It also warns me not to envy people who seem to succeed overnight. This year it will guide how I prepare for examinations and how I learn new words.
writing.expectedLength: A motto plus one well-organised explanation paragraph

items: Motto: "A quiet effort repeated every day outweighs a loud promise made only once."

Explanation: I chose this motto because perseverance matters more to me than sudden bursts of motivation that fade after a week. When I struggled with fractions in maths, it was not one long study session that helped me, but ten short ones spread across a month. The motto reminds me that every milestone is really just the last of many small, unnoticed steps. It also warns me against envying classmates who seem to succeed without effort, since I usually discover later that they worked quietly too. This year it will guide how I revise for tests, a little each evening instead of everything the night before.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote an original one-sentence motto; explained its meaning and origin in a full paragraph; connected it to my own school choices; used three unit vocabulary words
writing.support: Start from a unit word you like, such as perseverance or integrity, and build the motto around what that word means to you.
writing.extension: Write a second, contrasting motto that a different character from the story might choose, and one sentence saying whose motto is wiser and why.

writing.title: Writing 4: Reflect and Improve
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Answer this question in one reflective paragraph of four to six sentences: what kind of person do you want to become, and what steps will you take to get there? Then return to one earlier piece of writing from this unit, revise three sentences using the editing checklist, and add a short note naming the one improvement you are proudest of and why it strengthens the piece.
writing.modelText: I want to become the kind of person who is trusted completely, because integrity outlasts every certificate. To get there, I plan to keep my promises even when they become inconvenient. I also hope to develop resilience by treating setbacks as information rather than defeat. Joining the debate club will build my confidence in speaking before others. Step by step, those habits will shape the adult I intend to be.
writing.sentenceStarter: I want to become the kind of person who...
writing.expectedLength: One reflective paragraph plus three revised sentences

items: Reflection: I want to become the kind of person who is trusted completely, because integrity outlasts every certificate a person can earn. To get there, I plan to keep my promises even when they become inconvenient, and I want to admit my mistakes quickly instead of hiding them. I also hope to build resilience by treating setbacks as information rather than defeat. Joining the debate club next term will help me practise speaking honestly in front of people who might disagree with me.

Revised sentences: Before: "I did okay in the group project." After: "I contributed two full sections to the group project and helped resolve a disagreement about the deadline." Before: "Mentors help you." After: "A good mentor does not hand you answers; a good mentor helps you discover them yourself." Before: "The story taught me a lesson." After: "The story taught me that courage and honesty often cost something in the moment but pay off later." The improvement I am proudest of is replacing "did okay", a vague phrase, with two specific actions, because specific evidence is far more convincing than a general claim.

writing.successCriteria: I answered the reflection question honestly in a full paragraph; named concrete steps; revised three sentences from earlier work; explained my strongest improvement
writing.support: List three qualities you admire in people around you, choose the two that matter most, and build your paragraph on those.
writing.extension: Turn your steps into a numbered six-month plan with one measurable milestone per month, written in complete sentences.

writing.title: Writing 5: The Mentor's Diary
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a diary entry from Mr. Nadir's point of view on the evening after the competition, in two paragraphs of at least four sentences each. Describe what he observed at the school hall, what he is proud of, and what the day taught him about mentorship. Use at least two passive voice sentences and two unit vocabulary words.
writing.modelText: What a day this has been. The hall was filled long before the first speech, and the judges were seated at the long table by nine. Nora was transformed: the truth was spoken plainly, and the audience was moved by her honesty. Amal won, yet the prize seems the smallest part of it. I am proud of them both, for courage wears two faces. Perhaps the real lesson was mine: mentorship is not the pouring of advice but the uncovering of what a young person is capable of.
writing.sentenceStarter: What a day this has been...

items: What a day this has been. The hall was filled long before the first speech began, and the judges were seated at the long table by nine o'clock sharp. Nora was transformed once she began speaking the truth plainly instead of the polished version she had rehearsed, and the audience was moved by her honesty. Amal won the competition, yet the prize seems the smallest part of what happened today.

I am proud of them both, for courage wears two very different faces: Amal's steady confidence and Nora's late, difficult honesty. Perhaps the real lesson was mine. I used to think mentorship meant pouring advice into a young person until they were full, but today I learned it is closer to uncovering resilience that was already there, waiting for the right moment to show itself.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote in Mr. Nadir's voice and past tense; described the competition day accurately; included two passive voice sentences; used two unit vocabulary words; ended with a reflection on mentorship
writing.support: Reread the final scene under the mango tree and note what Mr. Nadir says about each girl before you begin.
writing.extension: Add a third short paragraph in which Mr. Nadir plans one concrete way the community centre will support both girls next term.

writing.title: Writing 6: Careers Information Text
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose one career mentioned in this unit, such as nurse, teacher, marine scientist, engineer or entrepreneur. Write a clear heading, then five accurate facts about the career in complete sentences: what the person does, the training or qualification required, one challenge, one reward, and how the community benefits. Write at least two of the five facts in the passive voice and use precise unit vocabulary throughout.
writing.modelText: Becoming a Marine Scientist. Marine scientists study the plants and animals that live in the ocean. A university qualification in biology or ocean science is usually required. Long weeks are often spent at sea in difficult weather, which tests a researcher's resilience. The reward is discovering knowledge that nobody held before. Coastal communities are protected by their research, because healthy reefs mean lasting supplies of fish.
writing.expectedLength: An organised information paragraph with a heading

items: Heading: Becoming a Primary School Teacher
Fact one (duties): A primary school teacher plans lessons, marks work and helps young children build the confidence to ask questions without fear.
Fact two (training, passive): A recognised teaching qualification is usually required, along with a period of supervised classroom practice before a teacher works alone.
Fact three (challenge): Managing a room of thirty different personalities at once is a genuine challenge, especially on days when several children need extra patience simultaneously.
Fact four (reward): The reward is watching a child who once struggled with reading suddenly finish a whole book on their own, a milestone few other jobs let you witness so directly.
Fact five (community benefit, passive): Whole communities are strengthened by good teachers, because every literate, confident adult in that community once sat in someone's classroom.
otherAnswers: A learner choosing engineer might write: "Engineers design and test structures such as bridges or water systems, and a university qualification in engineering is normally required."
A learner choosing entrepreneur might describe the challenge of managing a first small business alone, and how local jobs are created once that business succeeds.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote a clear heading; gave five accurate facts covering duties, training, challenge, reward and community benefit; wrote two facts in the passive voice; used precise unit vocabulary
writing.support: Reuse facts from “Building a Future” or the interview with Nurse Sana, rewriting each one in your own words.
writing.extension: Add a two-sentence “Is it for you?” section that asks the reader a question using an adjective + preposition phrase.

teacherNotes.note: Model disciplinary language aloud, teach annotation and source checking explicitly, use mixed-response modes, and give specific feedback on evidence, cohesion, viewpoint and vocabulary precision while increasing learner independence.

Encourage learners to use the AI tutor throughout the unit: to quiz themselves on the twenty-three vocabulary words, to drill adjective + preposition partners, verb patterns and the passive voice, to rehearse the career presentation and the five-minute success speech aloud, and to check comprehension answers against “Building a Future” and “The Storm of Truth”. grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Success, Careers, and Personal Growth" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 11-12 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'ambition'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "Building a Future" was about in their own words, and what happened in "The Storm of Truth, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Adjective + Preposition — The Basics" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.
